paragraphs.text: Hillside Community Orchard — volunteer days. The orchard on Mill Lane has 120 fruit trees, mostly apples and pears, planted by local residents on a former council field fifteen years ago. It is looked after entirely by volunteers, who meet on the first and third Saturday of each month from 10 am until about 1 pm. Nobody needs experience; the tasks are explained at the start of each session, and there is always someone who has done them before.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: What we do depends on the season. In winter we prune the trees and repair fences, in spring we plant new trees and cut the grass, and in late summer and autumn we pick the fruit. Tools and gloves are provided, but please wear boots and clothes you do not mind getting dirty. Children over eight may come with an adult who stays with them throughout.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Volunteers may take home a share of the fruit they pick, and the rest is sold at our apple day in October, with the money going towards new trees and equipment. Sessions are cancelled in heavy rain or strong wind; check the noticeboard at the gate or our message group before setting out. If you would like to join, just come along on a session day and ask for Maria, who keeps the list of volunteers.
paragraphs.label: C

texts.label: B
texts.title: Films in the Park — August screenings

paragraphs.text: Friday 2 August — family classic. Our first screening is a much-loved animated adventure suitable for all ages. Gates open at 7 pm and the film starts at dusk, around 8.45 pm. Bring blankets or low chairs; high-backed chairs must be used at the back so that everyone can see. Entry is free, but a collection will be taken for the children’s hospital.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Saturday 10 August — silent comedy with live music. A selection of short comedies from the 1920s, accompanied by a pianist playing on the bandstand. Tickets cost £5 and are available online only, as numbers are limited to 300. The screening lasts about ninety minutes, including a short interval.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Friday 16 August — science fiction double bill. Two films back to back, starting at 8.30 pm and finishing after midnight. Recommended for ages 12 and over. Food stalls will stay open until the end of the second film, and tickets at £8 include a free hot drink at the interval.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Saturday 24 August — audience choice. Vote online before 17 August for one of three recent films; the winner will be announced on our website. This screening will have subtitles throughout, and a signing interpreter will introduce the evening. Entry is free, and dogs are welcome on leads.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Using the staff kitchen. The kitchen on the second floor is shared by around ninety people from four departments, and it works only if everybody follows a few simple rules. It is open from 7 am to 7 pm; outside those hours it is locked by security. Tea, coffee and milk are provided free of charge and are restocked every Monday and Thursday morning; if something runs out between deliveries, tell reception rather than buying more yourself. Please keep noise to a minimum, as the kitchen is next to two meeting rooms.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The fridge is emptied every Friday at 4 pm, and anything left inside, whether labelled or not, is thrown away. Please label food with your name and the date, and keep it in a sealed container. The top shelf is reserved for items that need to be kept separate, such as food for staff with allergies, and nothing else should be placed there. If you keep medicine that needs to be refrigerated, use the small labelled box on the door shelf.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Wash, dry and put away anything you use straight away; the dishwasher is for mugs and plates only, not for pans or plastic boxes, which can melt. The person who fills the dishwasher last in the day is asked to switch it on before leaving. Microwaves are cleaned by the cleaning team each evening, but please cover food while heating it and wipe up any spills.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Recycling bins are under the sink: paper and card in the blue bin, cans and plastics in the green one, and food waste in the small grey caddy, which is emptied daily. If you notice a fault with any appliance, report it through the facilities helpdesk; do not try to repair it yourself. Complaints about other people’s behaviour in the kitchen should go to your line manager, not to the person directly. The kitchen rules are reviewed every six months by a group of volunteers from each department, who welcome suggestions.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Your annual performance review. Every employee has a review once a year with their line manager, normally in the month in which they joined the company. The review looks back at the previous twelve months and agrees objectives for the next twelve. It is not a disciplinary meeting, and problems with performance should never be raised for the first time at a review; they should have been discussed as they arose. Staff who have been with the company for less than a year have their first review at the end of their probation period instead.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Two weeks before the meeting you will receive a self-assessment form. Complete it honestly and return it to your manager at least three working days before the review, so that they have time to read it. You may ask colleagues you have worked closely with for brief written comments, which you can attach to the form, but this is optional. The form asks what went well, what was difficult and what support you would find useful.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The meeting itself usually lasts about an hour. Your manager will discuss your self-assessment, give feedback and agree between three and five objectives with you for the coming year. You will also discuss training: any course you and your manager agree would be useful is recorded on the form and passed to the learning team, who will contact you to arrange it. The meeting should be held in a private room, not at your desk.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: After the meeting, your manager writes a summary, which you will receive within ten working days. You may add your own comments before signing it. If you disagree with the summary and cannot resolve the matter with your manager, you may ask for a second meeting with your manager’s manager. The signed summary is kept in your personnel file for three years. Your objectives can be changed during the year if your role or priorities change significantly.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Laughter is so familiar that it rarely seems to need explaining. People laugh when something is funny, the assumption goes, and the more amusing the joke, the louder the laugh. Researchers who have actually counted when people laugh have found that this account is largely wrong. Most laughter in everyday conversation follows remarks that are not funny at all, such as greetings, questions and ordinary comments, and the person most likely to laugh is not the listener but the speaker. Laughter, it seems, is less a response to humour than a way of managing relationships. The difference matters, because it changes what laughter is thought to be for.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The evidence comes from studies in which observers recorded laughter in public places, noting who laughed, when and after what. In one well-known study, fewer than a fifth of the remarks that preceded laughter were judged to be even mildly humorous. Laughter also turned out to be highly social: people were around thirty times more likely to laugh when they were with others than when they were alone, and they laughed alone mostly when watching or reading something, which provides a kind of imagined company. Women laughed more than men in most of the conversations observed, and listeners laughed more when the speaker was a woman, though the reasons for this pattern are still debated.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Laughter is also far older than language. Chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans produce a panting sound during play, particularly when being tickled or chased, and the sound is clearly related to human laughter, though it is produced differently: apes laugh on both the in-breath and the out-breath, while humans laugh almost entirely while breathing out. Similar play sounds have been recorded in other mammals, including rats, which produce high-pitched calls when tickled by researchers. The origin of laughter, on this evidence, lies in signalling that rough play is not a real attack. Recordings of ape laughter played to human listeners are often recognised as laughter, even by people who have never seen an ape.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: That origin helps explain why laughter remains so closely linked to play and to reassurance. When one person laughs during a tense conversation, the laughter signals that no offence is intended and that the relationship is secure. Researchers have found that friends laugh together more than strangers, and that people adjust their laughter to match the person they are speaking to. A listener who laughs at a remark by a superior may be showing agreement or respect as much as amusement, which is why laughter can be used to flatter as well as to connect. Laughter, in this sense, works less like applause than like a handshake.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Not all laughter is the same, and listeners are surprisingly good at telling the difference. In experiments where people heard recordings of spontaneous and deliberate laughter, they could usually distinguish the two, and the spontaneous kind was consistently rated as more pleasant. Brain imaging suggests that the two are produced by partly different systems, and that hearing deliberate laughter causes listeners to work harder to understand what the laugher intends. Spontaneous laughter, by contrast, appears to be contagious: hearing it makes others more likely to laugh even when they do not know the reason. Actors trained to produce convincing laughter on demand still rarely fool attentive listeners for long.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The contagious quality of laughter has been exploited for a long time. Early radio and television comedy programmes added recorded laughter to make audiences at home more likely to find the material funny, and studies have shown that such laughter does increase how amusing viewers rate a joke, though the effect is smaller for jokes that are already very good. The practice has become less common in recent decades, partly because many viewers find it irritating and partly because tastes in comedy have changed. Live studio audiences, whose laughter is real, have largely replaced it.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Claims about the health benefits of laughter should be treated with more caution. Laughing raises the heart rate, deepens breathing and may temporarily increase tolerance of pain, possibly through the release of the body’s own pain-relieving chemicals. Some studies have linked a sense of humour with lower stress, but most have been small, and it is difficult to separate the effects of laughter from those of the social contact that usually accompanies it. The popular belief that laughter strengthens the immune system rests on very limited evidence. Researchers in the field generally recommend laughter for its social value rather than as a treatment.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: What emerges is a picture of laughter as an ancient social tool that humour has borrowed rather than created. People laugh to show that they are friendly, that they understand, that a threat is not serious or that they belong to a group, and they laugh at jokes partly because jokes are one of the situations in which these messages are most useful. Understanding laughter in this way does not make jokes less enjoyable, but it does suggest that the question of why something is funny may be less important than the question of who we are laughing with. The joke, in this view, is often just the excuse.
paragraphs.label: H
